extracted.intended_audience: educated public, parliamentarians, and policymakers concerned with war, peace, and national finance (18th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing political/economic pamphlets and the soundness of their arguments about war, peace, and public finance; focused on evidence, accounting, and practical policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability (requisite of a good peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peace must be stable — the treaty should provide real, adequate security that the peace will last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the treaty furnishes sufficient security (not merely a chance or contingent advantage). Question claims that future or hypothetical conquests provide security. Check whether possession of territories actually confers negotiation leverage or merely illusory dependence (examples: restored French islands, Pensacola vs. Havannah). Beware arguments that assume security based on inconsistent premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indemnification/Compensation (requisite of a good peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: After an expensive war, the peace should secure compensation (indemnification) — acquisitions or arrangements that will materially help defray the public expense and reduce debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether new territorial acquisitions or treaty terms yield revenue (customs, duties, trade) sufficient to aid the exchequer. Consider concrete alternatives the negotiator could have pursued (examples: possession of Guadaloupe or Martinico, renewal of the Assiento) and whether those would have produced 'floods of treasure' to the treasury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alliance (requisite of a good peace)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good peace should secure or strengthen alliances and avoid legitimizing or strengthening hostile confederacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether negotiations preserve or gain allies, or instead alienate existing allies and recognize or abet an enemy league (example: the Family Compact between Spain and France). Treat negotiators' interactions with allied/hostile powers as evidence: did they take steps to invalidate hostile alliances or did they negotiate as if separate crowns were independent when they were coordinated?

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of claimed conquests/security
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that future conquest or occupation will restore lost possessions or guarantee security must be supported by practical evidence of feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify such claims with public experience and military/practical testimony (consult commanders). Consider logistic, climatic, and human costs (e.g., unhealthy climates, loss of people) — a 'most successful enterprise' may still not compensate national losses. Do not accept bare assertions that territories can be 'taken whenever we think proper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's principles and arguments should be coherent and consistent across the work; avoid shifting standards from page to page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for contradictions (e.g., treating conquests as both insignificant and as providing perfect security). Flag when the writer applies different premises when convenient, and require consistent application of the same criteria throughout the pamphlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess timing of peace by terms actually obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether peace was made at the 'right time', evaluate whether the terms obtained were adequate to the nation's advantages and necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on abstract statements about 'secrets' of foreign cabinets. Instead, judge timing empirically by whether terms achieved match strategic goals. Authors should examine correspondence or negotiation records if they use timing as a critique; sarcasm about Parliamentary access to correspondence is not a substitute for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate accounting and correct debt categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Public debt accounting must correctly identify which items carry interest and must not double-count the same charge under different headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare itemized lists and the interest they actually carry (examples: exchequer bills, navy debt portion carrying interest). Do not compute interest on a principal that includes non-interest-bearing items, and do not include both interest and the 'deficiency of funds' that arises from that same interest charge (avoid double-charging). Use primary sources (parliamentary journals, authoritative tables) when asserting totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparable accounting periods and correspondent articles
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing expenditures across periods, ensure the items included are the same kinds and that incomparable items (deficiencies, extraordinary grants) are excluded or adjusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make 'apples-to-apples' comparisons by deducting items from one period that were not part of the base period (example: deduct deficiencies of land and malt, and fund deficiencies from a later peace establishment before comparing with an earlier peace establishment). Provide the exact items and arithmetic so readers can verify the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide proofs for numerical assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical claims and large round figures must be accompanied by evidence, sources, and detailed breakdowns—assertions alone are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require the author to cite primary sources (e.g., the 'Considerations' or House of Commons journals) and to give the states or tables referenced. Flag when an author 'asserts without proof' or refers to numbers without supplying the comparative statements needed to verify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical trade and manufacturing statistics to test economic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about decline or growth in trade and manufacture should be tested against concrete data (registries, excise returns, export/import totals) across comparable periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-year averages and region-specific registers (examples: pieces of cloth entered in West Riding of Yorkshire across three-year periods; averages of net excise receipts for comparable multi-year spans). Assess whether quantities and revenues rose or fell, and distinguish cyclical variation from trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate export categories when judging customs-entry accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in customs entries affect certain classes of exports (free goods) more than others; reliable categories exist (certificate goods/re-exports with drawback).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adjusting balances for presumed inaccuracy, limit allowances to the classes actually prone to error (free goods). Do not make blanket deflations of the whole balance when only a portion (at most two-thirds of home products free of drawback) is vulnerable; treat certificate goods as reliable because exporters must specify quantities to claim drawback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess tax impact via branch-specific revenue comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether new duties harmed consumption, compare the net produce of the same excise branches across comparable periods rather than general impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate averages of net excise receipts for specific branches across multi-year periods before and after duties (examples: hereditary and temporary excise averages, barrels of strong beer brewed before/after malt and beer duties). Use these comparisons to judge whether consumption fell or rose under new impositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose concrete, actionable remedies for public debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnoses of debt problems should be accompanied by realistic measures that could have materially reduced the public burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a commentator proposes practical steps (e.g., securing revenue-yielding territories, renewing profitable trading rights like the Assiento, pursuing policy to increase trade revenue) rather than only abstract admonitions on economy. Criticize works that alarm but offer no 'single light' toward reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical obfuscation and scare tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments should not rely on emotional or theatrical language that masks lack of evidence (e.g., conjuring 'ghastly phantoms' or invoking fear to substitute for proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer calm, evidence-based exposition over sarcastic jests or rhetorical fog. Flag uses of spectacle (mock-terrifying imagery, mystical appeals) as signs the argument may lack substantive support. Require sober appraisal of 'dreadful' scenarios with data rather than imaginative embellishment.
